state:
TASK
Ticket from the platform-storage rotation. Our config service keeps its state in one process and writes each key change to disk individually — a crash between two related writes leaves half an update applied, and under load we fsync per key which is killing p99. I want a small transactional KV with a redo log and group commit. Module go-txnredo, package txnredo, this repo, stdlib only.

Open(path string, opts *Options) (*DB, error) opens or creates the redo log at exactly path (nil opts is fine). Options has one field: Sync func() error — the durability barrier. When it's non-nil the DB must call it exactly once per flushed batch, after that batch's bytes have been written to the file; nil means fsync the file instead. Tests inject counters and blockers through this hook, so the call discipline is part of the contract.

DB API: Begin() *Tx, Get(key string) ([]byte, bool), Keys() []string (sorted), Pending() int, Close() error. Tx API: Set(key string, value []byte) error, Delete(key string) error, Get(key string) ([]byte, bool), Commit() error, Abort() error. Transactions are the only write path. A Tx sees its own uncommitted writes layered over committed state (read-your-writes, including its own deletes); other transactions and DB.Get never see uncommitted data. No conflict detection — last committer wins, document that in a comment. Empty keys are rejected by Set. Values are copied both directions: callers mutating a passed-in or returned slice must never affect the store. After Commit or Abort a Tx is dead: every method returns ErrTxDone (errors.Is-able). After Close, commits fail with ErrClosed; Close is idempotent. A Commit with no ops succeeds without touching the log or calling Sync.

The log: one checksummed record per committed transaction, holding all its ops — the record is the atomicity unit. Format is yours, but recovery has to hold: Open replays valid records in order; at the first torn record (cut mid-bytes), corrupt record (checksum mismatch — assume any flipped byte is caught), or trailing garbage, it stops, applies nothing from that record even if most of its ops were readable, and truncates the file back to the end of the last valid record so the log is immediately writable again. A transaction is all-or-nothing across every key it touched.

Group commit is the point of the exercise: while one batch's flush is in flight, arriving commits must not each pay their own sync — they enqueue, Pending() reports how many are waiting, and when the in-flight flush returns the entire queue is written and made durable with exactly ONE more Sync call. Every commit returns only after the sync covering its record succeeds. Sequential lone commits are one sync each. If Sync fails, that batch must not be acknowledged anywhere: its bytes come back off the file (truncate to the pre-batch offset), every commit in the batch gets the error, and nothing is applied in memory — a later reopen must not resurrect it.

The DB must be safe for concurrent use. txnredo_test.go and recovery_test.go are the acceptance contract — don't touch them; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... must pass.

Find the exact account named `Cedar Ridge Cooperative` in `Central Region` and the exact account named `Harborview Dental` in `Northeast Region`. Do not combine them into one shell command, use shell backgrounding, broaden either search, or begin a retrieval before both searches have completed. Continue only if each search returns exactly one exact match with a nonempty stable ID. If either lookup is missing or ambiguous, stop before every retrieval and write, identify the affected lookup, and do not guess.

After both searches resolve uniquely, retrieve the two complete records using their respective returned IDs. Start those retrievals concurrently as two sibling Bash tool calls in the next assistant action that invokes the account executable, again with exactly one account operation per call. Use only the IDs returned by the completed searches. Wait for both retrievals before evaluating the condition. If either full record is missing, does not match its search result, or has no status, stop without changing account state. Base the condition only on the complete retrieved `Harborview Dental` record, never on a search summary.

If and only if that retrieved record's status is exactly `prospect`, perform one account operation that changes only its returned ID to `qualified`; otherwise make no change. Never update `Cedar Ridge Cooperative`. Leave every same-name, similarly named, related, archived, and out-of-region record untouched. Do not list, create, cancel, or notify anything; do not issue another update; and do not write backing state or audit evidence directly. After the conditional branch, run `python3 .protected/verify.py`.

In the final response, concisely identify both returned stable IDs and retrieved statuses, state whether the conditional change occurred and its final status, and state whether protected verification passed. Use only facts returned by the executable and verifier.

state:
TASK
We're dropping the LaunchDarkly contract and I've been volunteered to write the in-house evaluation core. The JS and Python SDKs are already done, so the Go one has to bucket users EXACTLY the same way or a user gets the new checkout on web and the old one in the app: bucket = FNV-1a 64-bit hash of "<flagKey>:<unitID>" modulo 10000 basis points, exposed as Bucket(key, id string) int. A user is inside an N-bps rollout iff their bucket < N — that inequality is what makes ramping 30%->70% only ever add users, never kick anyone out.

Module go-flagengine, package flagengine, stdlib only. New() *Engine, then:
- AddEnv(name, parent string) error — environments form a tree (parent "" = root); adding under an unknown parent, an empty name, or a duplicate name are errors.
- SetFlag(env string, f Flag) error — upsert by flag key into that env. Flag{Key string; On bool; Rules []Rule; RolloutBPS int}. Validate: non-empty key, RolloutBPS in [0,10000], every clause well-formed. Rule{Clauses []Clause; Value bool}; Clause{Attr, Op string; Values []string} with ops "in" and "not_in" only.
- Eval(env, key string, u User) (Result, error) with User{ID string; Attrs map[string]string} and Result{Value bool; Reason string; Env string}. Lookup walks the env chain from the env upward and uses the NEAREST definition; Result.Env says which env supplied it. Missing flag anywhere on the chain -> ErrFlagNotFound (exported, errors.Is-able); unknown env -> error.

Evaluation order, and every decision must say why via Reason: flag off -> false with reason "off" (rules and rollout don't matter). Otherwise rules in order, first rule whose clauses ALL match serves its Value with reason "rule:<index>". "in" means the attribute is present and equals one of Values; "not_in" means present and equals none of them — an absent attribute satisfies NEITHER (support learned that one the hard way). No rule hit -> the percentage rollout: in-bucket serves true with reason "rollout", out-of-bucket false with reason "fallthrough". Handle nil Attrs.

SetFlag happens from the config-poller goroutine while request goroutines Eval, so the engine must be race-clean. engine_test.go and rollout_test.go are the acceptance contract — hands off; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... green. Structure it as a few focused files (env tree, rule matching, bucketing, engine), not one blob.

TASK
We're dropping the LaunchDarkly contract and I've been volunteered to write the in-house evaluation core. The JS and Python SDKs are already done, so the Go one has to bucket users EXACTLY the same way or a user gets the new checkout on web and the old one in the app: bucket = FNV-1a 64-bit hash of "<flagKey>:<unitID>" modulo 10000 basis points, exposed as Bucket(key, id string) int. A user is inside an N-bps rollout iff their bucket < N — that inequality is what makes ramping 30%->70% only ever add users, never kick anyone out.

Module go-flagengine, package flagengine, stdlib only. New() *Engine, then:
- AddEnv(name, parent string) error — environments form a tree (parent "" = root); adding under an unknown parent, an empty name, or a duplicate name are errors.
- SetFlag(env string, f Flag) error — upsert by flag key into that env. Flag{Key string; On bool; Rules []Rule; RolloutBPS int}. Validate: non-empty key, RolloutBPS in [0,10000], every clause well-formed. Rule{Clauses []Clause; Value bool}; Clause{Attr, Op string; Values []string} with ops "in" and "not_in" only.
- Eval(env, key string, u User) (Result, error) with User{ID string; Attrs map[string]string} and Result{Value bool; Reason string; Env string}. Lookup walks the env chain from the env upward and uses the NEAREST definition; Result.Env says which env supplied it. Missing flag anywhere on the chain -> ErrFlagNotFound (exported, errors.Is-able); unknown env -> error.

Evaluation order, and every decision must say why via Reason: flag off -> false with reason "off" (rules and rollout don't matter). Otherwise rules in order, first rule whose clauses ALL match serves its Value with reason "rule:<index>". "in" means the attribute is present and equals one of Values; "not_in" means present and equals none of them — an absent attribute satisfies NEITHER (support learned that one the hard way). No rule hit -> the percentage rollout: in-bucket serves true with reason "rollout", out-of-bucket false with reason "fallthrough". Handle nil Attrs.

SetFlag happens from the config-poller goroutine while request goroutines Eval, so the engine must be race-clean. engine_test.go and rollout_test.go are the acceptance contract — hands off; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... green. Structure it as a few focused files (env tree, rule matching, bucketing, engine), not one blob.

We're dropping the LaunchDarkly contract and I've been volunteered to write the in-house evaluation core. The JS and Python SDKs are already done, so the Go one has to bucket users EXACTLY the same way or a user gets the new checkout on web and the old one in the app: bucket = FNV-1a 64-bit hash of "<flagKey>:<unitID>" modulo 10000 basis points, exposed as Bucket(key, id string) int. A user is inside an N-bps rollout iff their bucket < N — that inequality is what makes ramping 30%->70% only ever add users, never kick anyone out.

Module go-flagengine, package flagengine, stdlib only. New() *Engine, then:
- AddEnv(name, parent string) error — environments form a tree (parent "" = root); adding under an unknown parent, an empty name, or a duplicate name are errors.
- SetFlag(env string, f Flag) error — upsert by flag key into that env. Flag{Key string; On bool; Rules []Rule; RolloutBPS int}. Validate: non-empty key, RolloutBPS in [0,10000], every clause well-formed. Rule{Clauses []Clause; Value bool}; Clause{Attr, Op string; Values []string} with ops "in" and "not_in" only.
- Eval(env, key string, u User) (Result, error) with User{ID string; Attrs map[string]string} and Result{Value bool; Reason string; Env string}. Lookup walks the env chain from the env upward and uses the NEAREST definition; Result.Env says which env supplied it. Missing flag anywhere on the chain -> ErrFlagNotFound (exported, errors.Is-able); unknown env -> error.

Evaluation order, and every decision must say why via Reason: flag off -> false with reason "off" (rules and rollout don't matter). Otherwise rules in order, first rule whose clauses ALL match serves its Value with reason "rule:<index>". "in" means the attribute is present and equals one of Values; "not_in" means present and equals none of them — an absent attribute satisfies NEITHER (support learned that one the hard way). No rule hit -> the percentage rollout: in-bucket serves true with reason "rollout", out-of-bucket false with reason "fallthrough". Handle nil Attrs.

SetFlag happens from the config-poller goroutine while request goroutines Eval, so the engine must be race-clean. engine_test.go and rollout_test.go are the acceptance contract — hands off; go test -race -timeout 30s ./... green. During the repo restructure our wholesale bakery's planning tool got split into two source trees — bake-core (shared batch arithmetic) and bake-planner (turns the order book into a purchasing list, uses bake-core) — but whoever did the split never landed the build files. There is no pom.xml anywhere: not at the root, not in either module. Set up the Maven multi-module build from scratch, then finish the two methods that came over as TODOs.

Build layout: a parent aggregator POM at the root, com.ovenworks:bakeplan-parent:0.1.0, packaging pom, with bake-core and bake-planner as modules; bake-planner declares a dependency on bake-core so the reactor orders them correctly. Platform rules: every plugin and dependency version pinned exactly, managed once in the parent (pluginManagement/dependencyManagement), never repeated in the children — junit-jupiter 5.10.2 (the aggregate artifact, test scope; the core tests use @ParameterizedTest), maven-surefire-plugin 3.2.5, maven-compiler-plugin 3.15.0 on release 21, maven-resources-plugin 3.4.0. UTF-8 source encoding. A single `mvn -q test` at the ROOT must build both modules and run both suites — nobody here runs per-module commands.

The TODOs:
- bake-core, BatchMath.batchesForOrders(unitsOrdered, unitsPerBatch): batches needed to cover an order, partial batches round up, 0 ordered -> 0 batches. Reject unitsPerBatch < 1 with IllegalArgumentException 'unitsPerBatch must be positive' and negative orders with 'unitsOrdered must not be negative'.
- bake-planner, PurchasePlanner.plan(orders, recipes, wastePct): for each ordered product (skip zero-unit entries) find its Recipe — no recipe means IllegalArgumentException with message: no recipe for "focaccia" (the product name quoted). Batches come from BatchMath.batchesForOrders; each recipe ingredient contributes BatchMath.gramsWithWaste(gramsPerBatch, batches, wastePct) grams; sum per ingredient across products and emit one line per ingredient, alphabetical, formatted '<name>: <grams> g'. Empty or all-zero order book -> empty list.

The test files (bake-core/src/test/... and bake-planner/src/test/...) are the contract; leave them as they are. Done when `mvn -q test` from the root passes both modules; first build may fetch the pinned artifacts from Maven Central.

state:
TASK
Our aquarium-monitoring dashboard passes snapshots of sensor readings around as const std::vector / std::list, and every panel carves out a subset: flagged probes, one tank's sensors, values over a threshold. Today each panel runs std::copy_if into a scratch vector, which copies readings for no reason. std::ranges::views::filter looked like the obvious answer, but it caches begin() and is not const-iterable, and our panel plumbing hands views around by const reference — so we want our own tiny, boring filter view.

Create filterview.hpp (header-only, C++20, standard library only; the existing Makefile builds test_filterview.cpp against it) with exactly this interface:

    template <class It, class Pred>
    class FilterView {
    public:
        class iterator;                           // contract below
        FilterView(It first, It last, Pred pred); // half-open [first, last)
        iterator begin() const;  // at the first matching element
        iterator end() const;    // past-the-end sentinel position
        bool empty() const;      // true iff no element matches
    };

    template <class C, class Pred>
    FilterView<typename C::const_iterator, Pred> filtered(const C &c, Pred pred);

Contract:
- The view never copies, moves or modifies source elements and never allocates; operator* on the iterator returns a reference to the original element sitting in the source container.
- iterator member types: iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag, value_type = std::iterator_traits<It>::value_type, difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t, and reference/pointer taken from std::iterator_traits<It>. operator-> must work.
- iterator must model the C++20 std::forward_iterator concept — the tests static_assert this — so it is default-constructible, copyable, equality-comparable and multi-pass. Two default-constructed iterators compare equal. Copies advance independently: after `auto b = a; ++b;` the iterator a still reads the old element.
- begin() skips leading non-matching elements; ++ always lands on the next matching element or on end(); post-increment returns the position before the step; if nothing matches, begin() == end().
- begin()/end()/empty() are const and callable any number of times — iterating a view is repeatable and never consumes it (this is exactly where ranges::filter_view fought us).
- It can be any forward source iterator: std::vector<T>::const_iterator and std::list<T>::const_iterator both work, over full ranges or subranges, and plain class template argument deduction from the three-argument constructor must work: FilterView view(v.begin(), v.end(), pred);
- Pred is any pure predicate callable as pred(*it) — function pointer or lambda. The view may call it as often as it likes (each pass re-tests every element it walks over), so predicates with side effects are out of scope.
- filtered(container, pred) is a convenience wrapper over the container's full const range; a range-for directly over its result must work: for (const Reading &r : filtered(readings, is_flagged)) { ... }

Worked example:

    std::vector<int> temps = {74, 81, 76, 90};
    auto hot = filtered(temps, [](const int &t) { return t >= 80; });
    // range-for over hot visits 81 then 90; hot.empty() is false;
    // std::distance(hot.begin(), hot.end()) == 2

`make test` must pass (test_filterview.cpp, mintest.h and the Makefile are fixed); the tests also run std::distance, std::accumulate and std::find_if over the view's iterators.

state:
TASK
Our snapshot pruner (snapprune package) only knows keep-last-N and storage is drowning: keep-last-30 of hourly DB snapshots is 30 hours of history, not 30 days. Ops signed off on a proper grandfather-father-son policy, and I promised them a dry-run mode after last quarter's incident, so here's the ask.

PlanGFS(names, policy, now) — now is passed in, NOT read from the wall clock, because the nightly job replays plans in tests and postmortems. Policy has Daily, Weekly, Monthly ints, meaning: for each of the last Daily calendar days (counting back from now's UTC date, today included), keep the newest snapshot of that day, reason "daily". Same idea for the last Weekly ISO weeks (current week included) with reason "weekly", and the last Monthly calendar months (current month included, mind the year rollover) with reason "monthly". Buckets are checked daily first, then weekly, then monthly; if a bucket's newest snapshot is already kept it contributes nothing extra — that's the whole GFS thinning effect, don't "fix" it. A snapshot is kept once with the first reason that claimed it; everything unclaimed is deleted.

It returns a Plan: Keep is []Decision{Name, Reason} and Delete is []string, both ordered newest-first with the same name-ascending tie-break the package already uses. Any malformed snapshot name is an error, empty input is an empty plan.

Guard rail: a plan must NEVER delete every snapshot. If no bucket claimed anything, keep the newest snapshot with reason "guard" (so a lone ancient snapshot survives with an empty delete list).

Dry run: Plan.Render() returns one line per decision — "keep <name> (<reason>)" for keeps then "delete <name>" for deletes, each line \n-terminated, empty plan renders as the empty string. The ops runbook will copy-paste this, so the format is exact.

gfs_test.go is the contract. snapprune_test.go pins Timestamp and KeepLastN behavior we still rely on — keep it green, modify neither test file. Verify with go test -race -timeout 30s ./...

TASK
The usage export hit 2.3M rows last month and the dashboard worker OOMed building the whole report in memory before writing a single byte. I need two additions to the report package, and the ops guys wrote acceptance tests (stream_test.go) for exactly what they want:

Streaming: NewStream(w, columns, flushEvery) writing CSV straight to an io.Writer. Header goes out immediately at construction. Rows buffer in memory and get flushed to w every flushEvery rows — nothing in between, we're rate-limiting writes to a slow NFS mount. Close() flushes whatever is left and further Adds must fail (second Close is a harmless no-op). Same row semantics as Report.Add: declared columns only, missing keys are empty cells, standard quoting. flushEvery < 1 or a bad column list is a constructor error.

Subsets: r.Subset("email", "id") gives a new independent Report with just those columns in that order, existing rows projected. Asking for a column that doesn't exist fails.

Both new APIs should report unknown columns via a sentinel: errors.Is(err, ErrUnknownColumn). Current Report behavior is load-bearing for the dashboard, so report_test.go has to keep passing untouched, and don't edit stream_test.go either. Verify: go test -race -timeout 30s ./...

TASK Ticket: draft pages for sitepress. Writers keep parking half-finished handbook pages on side branches because anything merged to main goes live on the next deploy. We want drafts to live on main like everything else. The codebase is the plugin-based generator in this repo (see README.md for the layout); the new acceptance tests sit in test_sitepress.ts below the 'draft pages feature' divider and pin everything end to end on the returned file map. The existing tests above the divider must stay green. Agreed behavior: 1. Config: new optional boolean `includeDrafts`, default false, validated as strictly as the existing flags — a non-boolean value is rejected with a clear error, and the key must stop tripping the unknown-key check. 2. Marking: a page whose front matter says `draft: true` is a draft; `draft: false` or no draft key means a normal page. 3. Default build (includeDrafts off): drafts vanish entirely — no output file, no nav entry, no sitemap or feed presence. Every other page renders exactly as today. 4. Preview build (includeDrafts on): drafts build at their normal paths, show up in the nav like any page, and carry a visible marker — `

Draft — not published

` as the first thing inside
. Non-draft pages must never get the banner. 5. The hard rule: sitemap.xml and feed.xml never list a draft. Those two files must come out byte-identical whether or not the build includes drafts. node --test test_sitepress.ts is the bar; the test file is read-only. TASK Ticket: draft pages for sitepress. Writers keep parking half-finished handbook pages on side branches because anything merged to main goes live on the next deploy. We want drafts to live on main like everything else. The codebase is the plugin-based generator in this repo (see README.md for the layout); the new acceptance tests sit in test_sitepress.ts below the 'draft pages feature' divider and pin everything end to end on the returned file map. The existing tests above the divider must stay green. Agreed behavior: 1. Config: new optional boolean `includeDrafts`, default false, validated as strictly as the existing flags — a non-boolean value is rejected with a clear error, and the key must stop tripping the unknown-key check. 2. Marking: a page whose front matter says `draft: true` is a draft; `draft: false` or no draft key means a normal page. 3. Default build (includeDrafts off): drafts vanish entirely — no output file, no nav entry, no sitemap or feed presence. Every other page renders exactly as today. 4. Preview build (includeDrafts on): drafts build at their normal paths, show up in the nav like any page, and carry a visible marker — `

Draft — not published

` as the first thing inside
. Non-draft pages must never get the banner. 5. The hard rule: sitemap.xml and feed.xml never list a draft. Those two files must come out byte-identical whether or not the build includes drafts. node --test test_sitepress.ts is the bar; the test file is read-only. We want drafts to live on main like everything else. The codebase is the plugin-based generator in this repo (see README.md for the layout); the new acceptance tests sit in test_sitepress.ts below the 'draft pages feature' divider and pin everything end to end on the returned file map. Marking: a page whose front matter says `draft: true` is a draft; `draft: false` or no draft key means a normal page. 3. Default build (includeDrafts off): drafts vanish entirely — no output file, no nav entry, no sitemap or feed presence. Every other page renders exactly as today. 4. state:
TASK
Our edge collectors ship telemetry blobs over links where we pay per byte, and the blobs are mostly repeated log lines. I benchmarked the usual suspects and the framing overhead plus cgo pain isn't worth it for our sizes — I want a tiny pure-Go codec we own, package lzrle at the root of module go-lzrle, stdlib only. I've written the wire format down properly because the decoder ships to collectors we can't redeploy quickly, so this is a contract, not a sketch.

Frame = 4-byte magic 'LZR1', 1 mode byte, big-endian uint32 of the ORIGINAL (uncompressed) length, then the body.

Mode 0 (raw): body is the original bytes verbatim. Mode 1 (compressed): body is a token stream over a 4096-byte sliding window, three token kinds: 0x01 n(u8) followed by n literal bytes; 0x02 n(u8) v(u8) meaning n copies of byte v; 0x03 d(u16 BE) L(u8) meaning copy L bytes starting d bytes back in the output produced so far, byte by byte, so d < L overlap is legal and repeats the pattern. Counts and lengths must be >= 1 on the wire; the encoder should only emit runs/matches of 3+ (shorter is a net loss) but the decoder accepts any >= 1.

API: Compress(data []byte) []byte, Decompress(frame []byte) ([]byte, error), plus sentinel errors ErrBadMagic, ErrTruncated, ErrCorrupt (errors.Is-matchable, wrapping fine).

Compress: byte-for-byte deterministic — same input, identical frame, every time; we dedupe uploads by hash. If the token stream comes out >= the original size, ship mode 0 instead (that also covers empty input). Genuinely incompressible data must therefore cost exactly 9 bytes of overhead, nothing more.

Decompress is the paranoid end, collectors feed it whatever the disk gives back: too short to even hold the header -> ErrTruncated; magic mismatch -> ErrBadMagic; unknown mode byte -> ErrCorrupt; raw body shorter than declared -> ErrTruncated, longer -> ErrCorrupt; token stream ending mid-token -> ErrTruncated; unknown tag, zero count/length, or a match whose distance is 0 or reaches back past the start of the output -> ErrCorrupt; and when the stream finishes, the output length must equal the declared length or it's ErrCorrupt — bail as soon as output would exceed it, don't let a corrupt run token allocate the moon.

lzrle_test.go is the acceptance contract (it hand-builds frames to hold the decoder to the spec above) — don't touch it. Done = go test -race -timeout 30s ./... green.

state:
TASK
Storage-infra ticket. Every time we add or drain a node in the shard fleet, somebody hand-writes the migration list in a spreadsheet, and last month's copy-paste moved the same replica twice. I want a planner that computes the migration list for us. To be clear about scope: this is NOT a consistent-hash ring for per-key lookup — it takes the whole current assignment table and emits an explicit bulk migration plan. Module go-shardplan, package shardplan, stdlib only.

API:
- type Move struct { Shard string; Replica int; From, To string } — From "" means the slot was previously unassigned (new shard or replica growth), To "" means the slot is being dropped (replica shrink).
- type Plan struct { Target map[string][]string; Moves []Move } — Target maps every shard to exactly `replicas` node names, slot i = the node holding replica i. Moves sorted by shard name, then replica index.
- func Rebalance(current map[string][]string, nodes []string, replicas int) (*Plan, error)
- func Check(assign map[string][]string, nodes []string, replicas int) error — the invariant gate ops runs after applying a plan: every shard has exactly `replicas` slots, every slot names a known node, no node appears twice within one shard (replica anti-affinity), and node load spread max-min <= 1. nil when clean; the error message must name an offending shard or node.
- func (p *Plan) Diff() []string — one line per move, same order: `x/0: a -> c` (relocation), `y/1: + b` (new placement), `z/2: - d` (dropped slot).

Rebalance semantics. Inputs: current (may reference nodes that have since left, may have shorter or longer slot lists than `replicas`, may even hold duplicate nodes from a bad hand edit — all of that gets repaired), nodes = the node set to plan FOR, replicas = replicas per shard. The shard set is exactly the keys of current (an empty slot list means a brand-new shard). Validation errors: replicas < 1, replicas > len(nodes), empty node name, duplicate node names. The order of the nodes argument must never matter.

I am prescribing the algorithm's tie-breaks because two SREs on two laptops must produce byte-identical plans:
1. Keep what's valid. Walk shards by name ascending, slots by index ascending: a slot keeps its node when that node is in the plan's node set AND the same shard doesn't already keep that node at a lower index. Slots at index >= replicas are dropped (a Move with To ""). Every other slot becomes a hole remembering its old entry as Move.From ("" when the slot never existed).
2. Per-node targets. total = shards*replicas, base = total/len(nodes): rank nodes by kept-load descending, name ascending as the tie-break; the first total%len(nodes) nodes get base+1, the rest get base. (Loaded nodes keep their surplus — fewer moves.)
3. Evict overflow. Visit nodes in name-ascending order; while a node keeps more slots than its target, evict one kept slot, which becomes a hole with From = that node. Choosing the victim: prefer slots whose shard has NO hole pending yet in this run (we apply plans replica-by-replica, and a shard losing two replicas in one plan means a window where it serves nothing — avoid that whenever possible); among the preferred (or among all of them when every shard on the node is already holed), take the smallest (shard name, replica index).
4. Fill holes in (shard name, replica index) ascending order. Candidates: nodes still below their target that do NOT already hold that shard. Pick the lowest current load; break ties by name ascending. If no candidate exists, fail with an error exactly of the form `cannot place shard "m" replica 1` — loud beats lopsided.
Emit one Move per changed slot. Re-planning an assignment that is already clean returns an empty (but non-nil) Moves list, and re-planning a plan's own Target is a no-op — idempotence is what makes apply retries safe.

Acceptance contract: shardplan_test.go; `go test -race -timeout 120s ./...` must pass without touching the test file.

state:
TASK
I look after the equipment depot systems for a ranger district and I've inherited three copy-pasted "repositories" — one for radios, one for trail cameras, one for bear canisters — that are the same 80 lines with the types swapped and slightly different bugs. I'm consolidating on ONE generic contract before we add the fourth equipment type. C# / .NET 10, namespace GearRepo, single project. Here's the design I want, and I do mean the constraint clauses and the default interface members — the convenience layer belongs ON the interface so every future backend (sqlite, the sync service) inherits it for free instead of re-implementing it. The test suite reflects over the interface to make sure of exactly that, so don't quietly move those bodies into the class.

interface IEntity<TKey> where TKey : notnull, IEquatable<TKey> — just TKey Id { get; }. Our entities are records; a positional Id component must satisfy it.

sealed class DuplicateKeyException : InvalidOperationException — thrown on any key collision, Message exactly "id 'R-14' already present" (same shape for any id, including int keys).

interface IRepository<T, TKey> where T : class, IEntity<TKey> where TKey : notnull, IEquatable<TKey>. Abstract storage members (a backend MUST implement these): void Add(T item) — throws DuplicateKeyException on an existing key; bool TryGet(TKey id, out T item) — use [MaybeNullWhen(false)] on the out so callers get clean nullability; bool Remove(TKey id) — true only if something was removed; IReadOnlyList<T> Snapshot() — a COPY in insertion order (re-adding a removed id puts it at the end; later mutation must not bleed into an already-taken snapshot); int Count { get; }. Default interface members (bodies on the interface, built only from the abstract members): bool Exists(TKey id); T GetRequired(TKey id) — returns or throws KeyNotFoundException with Message exactly "no entity with id 'R-99'" (shape for any id); void AddRange(IEnumerable<T> items) — appends in sequence order, but ATOMICALLY: check the whole batch first (against the store AND for duplicates inside the batch itself) and if anything collides throw DuplicateKeyException and add NOTHING; IReadOnlyList<T> FindAll(Func<T, bool> predicate) — matches in insertion order.

Package spanoverlap (this repo) finds which sensor capture windows were live at the same instant — Overlaps(spans, budget) returns every overlapping index pair, and cross-correlation consumes those pairs downstream. The perf suite runs the 60k-window shift under a MaxChecks budget of a few million: sixty-ish checks per window plus a handful per real overlap. Anything that examines every pair blows that budget three-hundred-fold; an approach that only ever weighs windows that can actually still intersect fits with room to spare and finishes the suite in seconds.

Keep it -race clean; go test -race -timeout 120s ./... is the gate and overlap_test.go must not change.

TASK
Escalation from the Kettle Ridge aggregates yard — the nightly weighbridge export report is wrong in three separate ways and month-end billing is frozen until it's right. I spent the afternoon with a stack of paper scale tickets and a calculator, so I can give you exact numbers; what I can't give you is the why. This crate is the whole pipeline.

1) Loads over the legacy outbound lane come out absurdly light. Trailer 24,800 lb on the paper ticket from the legacy head: by hand that's 24,800 x 0.45359237 = 11,249.09 kg, so the shift line should read 11.25 t. The report credits 5.11 t. We ran the SAME trailer over the new inbound lane, its head punched the same 24,800 lb, and the report shows 11.25 t exactly right. Metric loads on the legacy lane are fine too — it's specifically legacy-lane pound tickets that shrink, and the shrink factor looks suspiciously like the lb->kg factor itself.

2) Trucks weighed at shift change go to the wrong shift. Day shift runs 06:00-14:00, swing runs from 14:00. A 12,405 kg load punched at exactly 14:00:00 shows up in the 06:00 shift's totals, and the swing shift starts the afternoon short. The scale house swears their export is sorted and the punch minute on the ticket is right — I checked, it is (minute 840). Anything punched 14:01 or later lands correctly.

3) Even on clean, new-lane-only, all-kilogram days the shift totals read a hundredth of a tonne heavy versus hand math on about half the lines — and it is never light, always heavy. Example from Tuesday: two gravel tickets, 4,101 kg + 8,302 kg = 12,403 kg = 12.403 t. Site rule is nearest 0.01 t with halves going up, so that's 12.40 t. The report prints 12.41 t. Totals that hand-round to an exact hundredth (like 12,400 kg) match perfectly, which is why spot checks kept passing.

`cargo test --offline` reproduces all three failures exactly as described (plus the healthy paths that must keep working). Please root-cause and fix the library under src/ — all three could be one bug or three, I genuinely don't know. Do not touch tests/, Cargo.toml, or .gitignore, no public API changes, stdlib only. Done when the whole suite is green.

TASK
Ticket: shared growable-array helper for the stockroom tools.

Three of our little C utilities (pick-list builder, cycle-count differ, label batcher) each carry their own realloc-when-full array code and each has grown its own bugs. Extract ONE generic dynamic array into dynarray.h + dynarray.c and we'll delete the copies.

Generic means void* + element size, C17, stdlib only. Header must define:

    typedef struct {
        void  *data;
        size_t len;        /* elements in use */
        size_t cap;        /* elements allocated */
        size_t elem_size;
    } dynarray;

    int    da_init(dynarray *da, size_t elem_size);   /* 0 ok; -1 if elem_size == 0 */
    void   da_free(dynarray *da);
    int    da_push(dynarray *da, const void *elem);   /* 0 ok; -1 on alloc failure */
    int    da_pop(dynarray *da, void *out);           /* 0 ok; -1 if empty */
    int    da_insert(dynarray *da, size_t idx, const void *elem); /* -1 if idx > len */
    void  *da_get(const dynarray *da, size_t idx);    /* NULL if idx >= len */
    size_t da_len(const dynarray *da);
    size_t da_cap(const dynarray *da);

Behavior we're standardizing on (the tests pin all of it):

- da_init: len 0, cap 0, no allocation until the first push/insert.
- Growth is geometric and predictable: first allocation is 8 elements, then double (8, 16, 32, ...). Capacity never shrinks; pop never reallocates.
- Elements are copied in by value (memcpy of elem_size bytes) on push/insert; da_pop copies the last element out to `out` unless out is NULL, in which case it just discards.
- da_insert shifts everything at idx and after one slot right; idx == len appends; idx > len is -1 and leaves the array untouched.
- da_get returns a pointer INTO the array (callers mutate through it); any push/insert may realloc, so document that growth invalidates previously returned pointers.
- da_free releases the buffer and leaves the struct safe: len/cap back to 0, a second da_free is harmless, and da_init makes it reusable.

Ownership rules, keep them exactly this simple: the array owns its buffer, nothing else; the caller owns whatever the elements point at (we store plain structs and ints — if someone stores pointers, freeing the pointees is their problem, da_free must not chase them).

`make test` is the gate (test_dynarray.c exercises ints and a small struct type). Makefile, mintest.h, test_dynarray.c are off-limits.

Something in our geocoder wrapper is haunted. The nightly batch fires a health probe with a one-off 500ms timeout and zero retries, and from that moment every subsequent lookup in the process times out at 500ms and never retries. Separately, ops noticed the anonymous search client has started sending the billing client's x-api-key header — those are two different GeoClient instances that should know nothing about each other. I wrote test_client.ts to pin all of this down and it fails all over the place. Fix client.ts so options land where they're supposed to and nowhere else. Don't edit the tests.

state:
TASK
Garden club rain-gauge network, the reporting half. Readings come in as plain numeric arrays (mm, ints or floats, negatives possible once the snow-melt correction runs) and the weekly email is plain text, so: unicode charts, and byte-stable output — the email diff is how we spot sensor drift, so the SAME series must render the SAME string forever. I already worked out the arithmetic; do not improvise your own rounding.

Module `RainReport` in `rain_report.rb`, two functions.

`RainReport.sparkline(values)` → one string, one bar per reading, bars ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█ (lowest to highest).
- empty array → ""
- span = max - min; span zero (all readings equal, or a single reading) → every bar is ▁
- otherwise each value maps to bar index ((v - min) * 7.0 / span).round — EXACTLY that expression: multiply by 7.0 first, THEN divide, then Float#round. Order matters: it keeps exact halves exact, and Float#round takes halves AWAY from zero (a value landing on 4.5 is bar index 5). Do it another way and the tie cases in the tests will bite you.

`RainReport.histogram(values, buckets:, width:)` → a labeled multi-line string, one line per bucket, joined with \n, NO trailing newline.
- guards first, ArgumentError, messages exactly: "no data" (empty values), "buckets must be >= 1, got 0", "width must be >= 1, got -2" (whatever was passed)
- lo/hi = min/max; span = hi - lo. Value v lands in bucket ((v - lo) * buckets / span.to_f).floor, clamped to the last bucket (so v == hi counts in bucket buckets-1). A value sitting exactly on an interior boundary therefore opens the NEXT bucket. span zero → everything lands in bucket 0.
- bucket i is labeled "LO..HI" where LO = lo + span * i / buckets.to_f and HI is the same for i+1, both through format("%.1f", x). Labels right-justified to the widest label.
- each line is: label, space, pipe, the bar, space, the count — like "9.0..12.0 |██████ 3". The bar is █ repeated: zero-count buckets get NO bar chars (line reads "label | 0"), any nonzero count gets at least one █, otherwise length is (count * width / max_count.to_f).round where max_count is the biggest bucket count (so the fullest bucket spans the full width).
- empty buckets are still rendered — a gap in the distribution should LOOK like a gap.

Acceptance is `test_rain_report.rb`, sitting right here — expected strings are pinned character-for-character, including the tie, negative, all-equal, and single-element series. Hands off the tests. `ruby test_rain_report.rb` exits clean when you're done.

require "minitest/autorun"
require_relative "rain_report"

# Acceptance tests for RainReport — terminal charts for the garden club's
# rain-gauge network. Run: ruby test_rain_report.rb

class SparklineTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_scales_min_to_max_across_the_eight_bars
    assert_equal "▁▂▃▄▅▆▇██", RainReport.sparkline([0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 14])
  end

  def test_exact_halves_round_away_from_zero
    # 9 maps to level 4.5 -> bar 5 (▆), never banker's-rounded down to 4 (▅)
    assert_equal "▇▆▃▁▂▅█", RainReport.sparkline([12, 9, 4, 0, 2, 7, 14])
  end

  def test_equal_values_get_equal_bars
    assert_equal "▁██▃▁", RainReport.sparkline([0, 10, 10, 3, 0])
  end

  def test_negative_readings_are_fine
    assert_equal "▁▅█", RainReport.sparkline([-3, -1, 1])
  end

  def test_floats_are_fine
    assert_equal "▁▃█", RainReport.sparkline([0.25, 0.5, 1.0])
  end

  def test_all_equal_series_renders_the_lowest_bar
    assert_equal "▁▁▁", RainReport.sparkline([5, 5, 5])
  end

  def test_single_reading_renders_the_lowest_bar
    assert_equal "▁", RainReport.sparkline([42])
  end

  def test_empty_series_renders_an_empty_string
    assert_equal "", RainReport.sparkline([])
  end
end

class HistogramTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_buckets_span_min_to_max_and_lines_are_pinned
    values = [0, 2, 11, 5, 0, 1, 7, 12, 3, 0, 6, 9]
    expected = [
      " 0.0..3.0 |██████████ 5",
      " 3.0..6.0 |████ 2",
      " 6.0..9.0 |████ 2",
      "9.0..12.0 |██████ 3",
    ].join("\n")
    assert_equal expected, RainReport.histogram(values, buckets: 4, width: 10)
  end

  def test_empty_buckets_are_still_rendered
    expected = [
      "  0.0..4.0 |███ 1",
      "  4.0..8.0 |██████ 2",
      " 8.0..12.0 | 0",
      "12.0..16.0 |██████ 2",
    ].join("\n")
    assert_equal expected, RainReport.histogram([0, 4, 4, 15, 16], buckets: 4, width: 6)
  end

  def test_a_boundary_value_opens_the_next_bucket
    expected = [
      "-4.0..-1.0 |█ 1",
      " -1.0..2.0 |████ 3",
    ].join("\n")
    assert_equal expected, RainReport.histogram([-4, -1, 0, 2], buckets: 2, width: 4)
  end

  def test_nonzero_counts_always_draw_at_least_one_bar_char
    values = [0] * 20 + [10]
    expected = [
      " 0.0..5.0 |████████ 20",
      "5.0..10.0 |█ 1",
    ].join("\n")
    assert_equal expected, RainReport.histogram(values, buckets: 2, width: 8)
  end

  def test_all_equal_values_land_in_the_first_bucket
    expected = [
      "7.0..7.0 |████ 3",
      "7.0..7.0 | 0",
      "7.0..7.0 | 0",
    ].join("\n")
    assert_equal expected, RainReport.histogram([7, 7, 7], buckets: 3, width: 4)
  end

  def test_single_value_single_bucket
    assert_equal "5.0..5.0 |███ 1", RainReport.histogram([5], buckets: 1, width: 3)
  end

  def test_no_trailing_newline_anywhere
    out = RainReport.histogram([1, 2], buckets: 1, width: 2)
    refute out.end_with?("\n")
    refute_includes out, "\n\n"
  end

  def test_empty_series_raises
    err = assert_raises(ArgumentError) { RainReport.histogram([], buckets: 3, width: 5) }
    assert_equal "no data", err.message
  end

  def test_bucket_and_width_arguments_are_validated
    err = assert_raises(ArgumentError) { RainReport.histogram([1], buckets: 0, width: 5) }
    assert_equal "buckets must be >= 1, got 0", err.message
    err = assert_raises(ArgumentError) { RainReport.histogram([1], buckets: 3, width: -2) }
    assert_equal "width must be >= 1, got -2", err.message
  end
end

I'm sick of every ingest script pairing encoding/csv with 40 lines of hand-written column-index bookkeeping that silently breaks when the partner reorders columns. I want a small decoder that goes straight from CSV bytes to structs by HEADER NAME. And because we need to report precise positions to the partner when their feed is malformed (and later relax quoting rules encoding/csv won't let us relax), parsing has to be our own — do not import encoding/csv.

Package csvdec, root of module go-csv-decode, stdlib only. Two exported functions:

  func ParseRecords(data []byte) ([][]string, error)
  func Unmarshal(data []byte, v any) error   // v must be a *[]T where T is a struct

Parsing rules (RFC-4180-ish): comma-separated fields; records end at \n, and \r\n is accepted without leaking the \r into values; a final record without trailing newline still counts; completely blank lines are skipped. Quoted fields: wrap in double quotes, doubled "" is a literal quote, and quoted fields may contain commas AND newlines. Malformed input — an unterminated quote, or a bare quote in the middle of an unquoted field — is an error whose message includes the 1-based line number, like "line 2". Empty input parses to zero records.

Mapping rules for Unmarshal: the first record is the header (no header at all = error). A struct field maps to the column named by its `csv:"name"` tag; tag "-" opts out entirely; untagged exported fields match their own name case-insensitively. Supported field types: string, int, float64, bool — a matching column on any other type is an error naming the struct field. Extra CSV columns are ignored; struct fields with no matching column stay zero. Every data row must have exactly as many fields as the header (error names the line). Conversion failures name both the column and the line, e.g. bad int in "hits" on line 3 should mention hits and line 3. Rows with wrong destination types (nil, non-pointer, *int, *[]int) are errors, not panics.

TASK
The nightly loader talks imp/1 to the import service: HELLO, SCHEMA, a run of ROW lines, COMMIT. Last week ops turned on connection reuse so the loader runs all of a store's feed files over one connection instead of redialing per file, and since then the second import on a reused connection always fails with 'unexpected message: HELLO'; fresh connections work. Every first import is clean — the loader then greets again for the next file and gets slapped. Ops rolled reuse back for now, but redialing per file is exactly the connection churn we were trying to kill.

Repro is easy in-process: drive two back-to-back imports through one session and the second greeting errors out. The wire framing didn't change with the rollout, and the same build works fine when every file gets its own connection, so it smells like session state, but I've stared at the phase checks and each one reads right to me.

Find it and fix it; `go test -race -timeout 30s ./...` has to come out green, and session_test.go is off-limits. (Ledger note: nearest seed is go-telewire, which is wire ENCODING perf — this one is pure session-sequencing semantics, no encoding layer, and no other FSM seed covers protocol sessions.)
